The Philadelphia 76ers were not considered a serious contender for LeBron James when NBA free agency began nearly a month ago. However, after making an aggressive trade for former Boston Celtic Jaylen Brown, Philadelphia opened up an entirely new opportunity for the organization.

After James remained quiet for more than three weeks, the decision was finalized Friday morning when he announced that he would finish his career in Philadelphia.

“LeBron James is signing with the Philadelphia 76ers for his final run at another NBA championship, he announced Friday,” ESPN’s Dave McMenamin wrote. “James, 41, is signing a two-year, $8 million contract with a player option, Klutch Sports Group CEO Rich Paul told ESPN's Shams Charania.”

The 76ers already have an impressive starting lineup and solid depth, but they could still look to add more pieces to the roster. One specific area of need is adding more defensive-minded players and reliable three-point shooters off the bench.

“The Philadelphia 76ers should prioritize defense and three-point shooting after LeBron James signed with the team this offseason,” Athlon Sports’ Paolo Songco wrote.

The 76ers are undoubtedly one of the favorites to win the Eastern Conference this upcoming season. Their roster is loaded with talent and difficult to overlook. It also does not appear that Philadelphia is finished making moves, as James’ former teammate Kentavious Caldwell-Pope is expected to join the team once he is officially bought out by the Memphis Grizzlies.

“Kentavious Caldwell-Pope is negotiating a buyout with the Grizzlies and intends to sign with the 76ers, per Chris B Haynes. KCP joins Bron in Philly,” Bleacher Report posted.

Caldwell-Pope is exactly the type of player the 76ers need off the bench, and he brings a wealth of championship experience. James and Caldwell-Pope won a championship together with the Los Angeles Lakers during the 2020 NBA bubble.

Caldwell-Pope has earned $147 million through his NBA contracts throughout his career. This is the type of move Philadelphia should make, and it is one James will certainly approve of. So far, after landing James, the 76ers are making all the right moves.

title: NBA superstar LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers
description: Basketball superstar LeBron James announces he will join the Philadelphia 76ers for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.
fullText:
LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.

The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.

The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumoured to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X.

James has won an NBA title with all three teams he previously played for. He won two with Miami, who earlier this week mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.

A Heat spokesperson told Reuters the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he played for between 2010 and 2014.

Either side of that Miami stint, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio.

"Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.

James helped the Cavs become NBA champions in 2016 and joined the Lakers in 2018, claiming another NBA title two years later.

He has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and has been an NBA All-Star the last 22 seasons running.

'Maybe he's a racist' - Trump critical of James

James said after last season that he was "pretty sure I [had] played my last game" but realised "I still truly love this game and I have more to give".

ESPN has reported that James has signed a two-year contract, with a player option for the second year, worth $8m (£6m). His average salary with the Lakers last season was $50.7m (£38m).

James added: "I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point?

"I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship."

The 76ers reached the Conference semi-finals in last season's play-offs, where they lost to the eventual champions, the New York Knicks.

They have since acquired Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics, in exchange for Paul George and some future draft picks.

title: NBA Trade Rumors: After LeBron James Decision, Massive Moves Ahead
description: NBA trade rumors are back in swing now that the league has gotten LeBron James' decision. He is heading to Philadelphia ... and now what? The post NBA Trade Rumors: After LeBron James Decision, Massive Moves Ahead appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Well that’s that. LeBron James has shocked the NBA and made a remarkable choice, opting to play for the Sixers for the next two years in a move that will have massive reverberations around the league. And we’re now ready to kick the old NBA trade rumor mill back into gear.

So what is coming next? We asked, let’s look …

James Harden. There was some question as to whether the Cavaliers would work as a unit if both Harden and James were on the team alongside Donovan Mitchell. Now, that won’t be an issue. But the Cavaliers now will have to finish up their summer with a contract for Harden and some sort of way to fill out the roster–they can add at least one more player, and they’ve been linked to DeMar DeRozan, Mario Hezonja and Jonathan Kuminga. Of note: The Cavs do want to give significant minutes to young players Meleek Thomas and Jaylon Tyson this season.

Draymond Green. The Warriors were holding off on signing Green in hopes of adding James. Now that James is off the board, the Warriors will give Green their remaining cap room but will still be on the lookout for another addition–they’re in the market for DeRozan and Hezonja. There’s an outside chance that the Warriors could move Moses Moody in a deal, and may have interest in Cam Johnson.

Peyton Watson. The Nuggets are still holding out hope to keep Watson in restricted free agency. Now that the James situation is settled, the Nuggets could finally seek to trade away Cam Johnson, who has not been the target that many expected thus far. The Nuggets have rebuffed interest in Johnson so far, but that could change.

Mario Hezonja. Hezonja has made his return to the NBA a notable one, as he has been one of the best players in the Spanish league after flaming out during three stops in the league after he’d been the No. 5 overall pick. Can Hezonja still play? That’s unclear but he’s done well to hype himself up as a contributor for contenders who are now bidding on his services.

Jonathan Kuminga. This has been the big donut in the coffee of the NBA offseason, and Kuminga remains the subject of sign-and-trade rumors. But the Hawks do not want players back, and will want some draft compensation no matter what. Can they get anyone to pay it? The Cavs are a longshot, as are the Lakers, and there are expected to be others in the mix.

DeMar DeRozan. He was waived by the Kings, and it is unlikely he will follow James to the Sixers. Miami? Cleveland? Warriors? His options are open.

Bradley Beal. The Miami Heat? That makes the most sense for Beal, who has been linked to the Celtics, Cavaliers, Warriors and others.

Bronny James. Will he join his father in Philadelphia? Many think he should stay in Los Angeles, including some with the Lakers who have liked his development. It should be time to sink or swim in the NBA for Bronny James, but if his dad wants him in Philly, that’s where he will go.

Well, no one expected Anthony Davis and Kyrie Irving to pop back up on the NBA market here in late July but, the rumor mill is never-ending. Neither is expected to get moved, but they’re still being talked about  …

Anthony Davis, Wizards. (Remaining contract: two years, $121 million, including player option.) Davis has been the subject of much speculation this offseason, but around the league, there isn’t a sense he is going to be dealt. The Wizards would like to get Davis on the floor and see if he can help them compete for a playoff spot. If not, he could be dealt by the February trade deadline.

Zion Williamson, Pelicans. (Remaining contract: two years, $87 million.) We’re not expecting Williamson to be moved by the end of the summer, but if he stays on the floor early in the year, New Orleans has plenty of incentive to find a new spot for him. A frontcourt of Derik Queen and Williamson makes little sense.

Kevin Durant, Rockets. (Remaining contract: two years, $90 million, player option.) There does not seem to be a market for Durant, who is 37 and has $90 million over two years on his contract. Rumors of Pistons interest has faded as the focus there is on re-signing Jalen Duren. Maybe a Durant deal comes back up after that gets done? It’s a longshot.

Jamal Murray, Nuggets. (Remaining contract: three years, $160 million.) The Nuggets are on track to operate over the second apron, which is not a place any team–especially a Kroenke team–likes to operate. Dealing Murray could shave some money off the cap but he was an All-Star last year and dumping him might be too much to ask of the Nuggets.

Jimmy Butler, Warriors. (Remaining contract: one year, $57 million.) It just does not appear that the Warriors are looking to move Butler. He’s the team’s main path to adding another star, as he is probably out until Christmas or later as he recovers from January ACL surgery. There are not many teams looking to add a rehabbing 36-year-old to their mix, and the Warriors are not likely to find a player who is better than Butler when healthy.

It’s hard to bring in a young star–or even a young potential star–on the trade market. But there could be some wrangling for these guys, the 25-and-under (OK, 26 for Trey Murphy) crowd.

Moses Moody, Warriors. (Remaining contract: two years, $26 million.) Moody him self said he is “curious” about what will happen to him on the trade market. Will James’ decision change that? He has developed into a valuable piece for Golden State, but a nasty knee injury could keep him out for most of next season.

Jalen Duren, Pistons. (Remaining contract: restricted free agent.) Sign-and-trade options for Duren are all but extinguished–were the Pistons ever really weighing a deal with the Kings for Domantas Sabonis? The Pistons have made moves to be able to give Duren more money, and that’s the likely way this all plays out.

Trey Murphy, Pelicans. (Remaining contract: three years, $88 million.) Murphy is a favorite in NBA trade rumors, but there are questions on how serious New Orleans would be about trading him. One exec says it will take a Desmond Bane-style offer (four first-round picks) to pry him from New Orleans, though that price has dropped a bit. Still, there’s been no movement yet.

Peyton Watson, Nuggets. (Remaining contract: restricted free agent.) The long restricted free-agent slog is on for Watson, and the Nuggets have surprised many by not being aggressive in moving players to create some breathing room to keep Watson. The sign-and-trade market reportedly includes the Clippers, Hawks and Bucks, but there is not much yet that would attract the Nuggets’ attention on a deal.

Nikola Jovic, Heat. (Remaining contract: four years, $62 million.) There is trepidation about trading for Jovic, who is certainly available and is still only 23 years old. But the remaining contract is a hefty bite for teams to take.

LeBron James will create an NBA trade rumor ripple effect, and the East could feel it most.

Michael Porter Jr., Nets. (Remaining contract: one year, $40 million, partial guarantee.) Porter is in the final year of his deal and wants an extension that starts at about what he is making now. The Nets likely won’t go that high, and if no middle ground is found, we are in for another heap of trade talk. Even if Porter is extended, he could be a trade candidate by next February’s deadline.

Grant Williams, Hornets. (Remaining contract: one year, $15 million.) The Hornets are not quite done with their roster, and Williams’ expiring deal has some value. He can still be a worthy big man off the bench.

Royce O’Neale, Hornets. (Remaining contract: two years, $21 million,) The Hornets would not be able to trade O’Neale with anyone else yet, so they could wait on a deal. But the team has gotten calls about moving him on after he’s come over from the Suns.

Jarrett Allen, Cavaliers. (Remaining contract: three years, $90 million.) As with Mobley, if the Cavs entice LeBron James to Cleveland, Allen could be trade bait. It’s more likely that Allen gets traded than Mobley, and the Cavaliers could get some relief and a contributor. Allen is a standard offensive center but is a valued rim-runner who can protect the paint.

Max Strus, Cavaliers. (Remaining contract: one year, $16 million.) The Cavs are trying hard to fit everything under the second apron, and that likely means moving off Strus, if they can find a taker.

Dennis Schroder, Cavaliers. (Remaining contract: one year, $14.6 million.) Schroder has played for 11 teams in the NBA so far, and the Cavs would be open to making it 12 as they seek to duck the second apron and still stay in the contending picture.

Myles Turner, Bucks. (Remaining contract: three years, $80 million.) Two things may well both be true on Turner–the Bucks are not shopping him because they want some veterans on hand, and there is no interest in him from other teams because of his contract.

Kyle Kuzma, Bucks. (Remaining contract: one year, $20 million,) His expiring contract is attractive and if the Bucks pull a sign-and-trade for Peyton Watson, Bennedict Mathurin or Jonathan Kuminga, he figures to be involved.

Jake LaRavia, Lakers. (Remaining contract: one year, $6 million.) Hustles, plays every game, but inconsistent. His contract makes him an attractive piece, though.

Herb Jones, Pelicans. (Remaining contract: four years, $82 million, including player option.) Jones is a popular name on the market, but the Pelicans are said to want two first-round picks, and with Jones having struggled with injuries and his 3-point shot in the past two seasons, that’s probably too steep. His remaining contract scares off potential suitors, too.

Derrick Jones Jr., Clippers. (Remaining contract: one year, $10 million.) Jones is a defensive ace still, and his expiring contract gives the Clippers some wiggle room to move him. They’re caught in the Aspiration pause, however.

Rudy Gobert, Timberwolves. (Remaining contract: two years, $74 million, including player option.) The Wolves, according to a report in The Athletic, were offered Jaylen Brown with the Celtics wanting Rudy Gobert, plus picks, as part of a trade package. The Wolves turned that down, though there still has been interest in Gobert, who is up for an extension.

Keldon Johnson, Spurs. (Remaining contract: one year, $17.5 million.) The reigning Sixth Man of the Year is heading into the final season of his contract, and San Antonio is likely to phase out his minutes in favor of younger players. He is still a valued leader on the team, but he could be a chip worth cashing in if the Spurs can land a first-round pick.

Domantas Sabonis, Kings. (Remaining contract: two years, $93 million.) Sabonis has had some nibbles, but no bites. There was a rumor that the Hornets were planning to trade for him, but that proved fruitless. Then there was the Jalen Duren sign-and-trade with the Pistons, which was far-fetched from the beginning. This one might have to wait until the season gets going.

Jrue Holiday, Blazers. (Remaining contract: two years, $72 million, with player option.) Certainly, something has to give in Portland with the arrival of Morant. Holiday is not getting any younger, but he has value around the NBA.

Zach LaVine, Kings. (Remaining contract: one year, $49 million.) LaVine picked up the player option worth $49 million. There was some hope that he could be waived, but after the Kings let DeMar DeRozan go, they’ll keep LaVine on the books and hope they can find a place to dump him.

Aaron Gordon, Nuggets. (Remaining contract: three years, $110 million.) Gordon has struggled to stay healthy, but is still a valued connective piece when he plays. He needs to be a No. 3/4 option on a good team, and teams aren’t falling over themselves to cough up assets for that, and the Nuggets have not pushed hard for a trade.

Daniel Gafford, Mavericks. (Remaining contract: 3 years, $54 million.) Gafford will be 28 in October, and with the Mavs focused on getting younger, moving him along has been one of the team’s top options. The concern is whether the guy the Mavs want to be their stalwart center–Dereck Lively II–can stay healthy. Lively has played 98 games in three seasons.

PJ Washington, Mavericks. (Remaining contract: 4 years, $90 million.) Like Gafford, Washington is aging out of the Mavericks’ timeline, as he turns 28 this summer. He’s a stretch 4 who plays good defense, but his shooting has been suspect–he made just 32.5% of his 3s last year. Washington’s extension kicks in this year, though, so he might be a better trade target down the line.

Klay Thompson, Mavericks. (Remaining contract: one year, $17 million.) Another aging Mav! Thompson does not fit Dallas’s timeline, and if the Mavs can get anything–youth, a few second-rounders–for him, they will. He’s still a 38% 3-point shooter. The addition of Tarik Biberovic is more incentive to move Thompson.

Cam Johnson, Nuggets. (Remaining contract: one year, $23 million.) Johnson has been a disaster in Denver, and he has been a prominent feature on the NBA trade rumor mill for years now. He still has enough of a reputation around the league to warrant trade interest, but a report from The Stein Line suggests the Nuggets are not going that route … yet.

The NBA trade rumor mill has had a busy summer, interspersed with some controversy. Here are the top rumors that sprouted into actual trades …

Boston’s controversial decision to move Brown as he neared an extension on a supermax contract set off a round of second apron discussion in the NBA.

Celtics get: Paul George, a 2028 first-round pick that could convert to a swap, Philly’s 2031 unprotected first-rounder, and two second-round picks.

The deal that kicked off the summer was the one most expected to be expanded, but wound up staying a two-teamer. The Bucks are banking on this being enough for a rebuild, and the Heat were hoping this precedes a LeBron James return. Alas …

Bucks get: Tyler Herro, Kel’el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kasparas Jakucionis go to Milwaukee. Also Bucks got the 13th pick in the draft (Nate Ament) and future first-rounders, in 2031 and 2033, plus a future pick swap and a second-round pick.

Heat get: Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis.

The Wolves combined their two major transactions, taking a chance on bringing in LaMelo Ball and getting off the contract of Julius Randle.

Timberwolves get: LaMelo Ball, Josh Green, No. 33 pick (Isaiah Evans).

Hornets get: Naz Reid, Mouhamadou Gueye, rights to Matteo Spagnolo, Minnesota’s first-round pick in 2033, second round picks in 2029, 2032 and 2033, plus three swaps, also from Minnesota.

Nets get: Julius Randle, No. 28 pick (Joshua Jefferson).

Memphis finally moves on from Ja Morant, and was able to do so by taking on Jerami Grant’s contract–but did not have to include outgoing draft capital.

Grizzlies get: Jerami Grant and Kris Murray.

A classic NBA deal that started as Isaiah Stewart going to Memphis, but ballooned since.

Grizzlies get: Isaiah Stewart, D’Angelo Russell, AJ Johnson, five second-round picks. (Lose: Santi Aldama.)

Pistons get: John Collins, Taurean Prince, Gary Harris. (Lose: Isaiah Stewart, Caris LeVert, Marcus Sasser.)

Clippers get: Trade exception. (Lose: John Collins.)

Wizards get: Khris Middleton. (Lose: D’Angelo Russell.)

Bucks get: Caris LeVert. (Lose: Taurean Prince, Gary Harris, AJ Johnson.)

Mavericks get: Santi Aldama, Marcus Sasser. (Lose: Khris Middleton.)

Now,  this trade has been undone punishment for the Aspiration scandal has yet to be doled out, but it’s still likely to get done once that situation is settled. There are still a lot of questions about when that might be, though.

Clippers get: Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks (2031 and 2033), plus a swap and two second-round picks.

The Hornets had been looking for a taker for Bridges, whose past domestic violence charges scared off many teams. But Charlotte attached draft capital and the Suns took him in.

Suns get: Miles Bridges, 2029 first-round pick, 2027 second-round pick.

Hornets get: Grayson Allen, Royce O’Neale, 2033 first-round pick.

The Thunder jettisoned Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins for second-round picks early in July, and got all the way under the second apron by moving Lu Dort later in a three-team deal that saw former No. 1 overall pick Zaccharie Risacher dealt, too.

Hawks get: Lu Dort, Ryan Nembhard.

Thunder get: Three second-round picks.

Mavericks get: Zaccharie Risacher.

title: Where former Oregon PG Payton Pritchard lands in redo of 2020 NBA Draft
description: Payton Pritchard has far outperformed his No. 26 overall draft spot, but just how far does he rise in a 2020 NBA redraft?
fullText:
During Payton Pritchard's first four seasons in the NBA, he was largely used as an end-of-the-bench reserve for the Boston Celtics. As the 26th pick in the first round in the 2020 NBA Draft after four seasons with the Oregon Ducks, he had slightly begun to live up to the late-first-round billing in Year 4, averaging 9.6 points for a Celtics team that won the title.

But the rise continued into the 2024-25 season when point guard Jrue Holiday was traded away, clearing a prominent bench role for the former Duck. Pritchard averaged 14.3 points and 3.5 assists while converting on 40.7% of his triples, winning the NBA's Sixth Man of the Year award.

Now coming off a season in which he started 50 games for Boston and averaged a career-high 17.0 points and 5.2 assists, it's clear that Pritchard has far outpaced his 26th overall spot in the 2020 draft.

But just how far up would he go in a 2020 redraft?

According to The Ringer's Bill Simmons, Pritchard would go 10th overall, only behind stars such as Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Tyrese Maxey and several others.

"Pritchard took a couple years," Simmons said during an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast. "I always liked him more than it seemed like the coaches liked him and it was always unclear why he wasn't getting the car keys a little bit more, and I think the team liked him because they gave him a contract even before he'd kind of become who he became. And then he just became one of the best bench guards in the league. Last year, he moved into a whole different level."

Heading into the 2026-27 season, Pritchard has a chance to move up yet another level. The Celtics traded away last years leading scorer Jaylen Brown, who took 21.7 shots per night. While Jayson Tatum and Paul George, who arrived via the Brown trade, will take some of those looks, the door is cracked open even more for an increased amount of Pritchard shots.

Already, Pritchard is making teams with picks in the 10's and early 20's of the 2020 draft wish they could've taken him, but that regret could reach an even higher mark in the seasons to come.

title: Why LeBron's new team — the 76ers! — should happily trade for Bronny James
description: If LeBron wants to continue playing with his son in the NBA, it should be a no-brainer for the 76ers.
fullText:
At long last, LeBron James has made his decision. The 41-year-old is a Sixer, signing a two-year deal worth $8 million to join Philadelphia.

For James' free agency, it's not clear what the exact terms of engagement were during this round. But unlike past courtships, the employment status of James' son Bronny will likely be part of internal discussions with LeBron's new team in Philly. In 2024, when James' Los Angeles Lakers selected Bronny with the 55th pick in the draft, the Jameses became the first father-son pairing to play in the NBA together.

LeBron has not publicly stated that he'd like his eldest son to join him, and it's not a given the Lakers would satisfy any such request. But it also wouldn't be a surprise to hear that LeBron would prefer to continue playing with his son. In the playoffs, after throwing an alley-oop to Bronny in a Game 3 win over the Houston Rockets, LeBron didn't hold back his joy.

"It just keeps getting better and better," he said after the game. "It's like, wow."

As of now, there is no plan or request for Bronny to join his father, per ESPN Ramona Shelburne. But that could always change as the season draws closer. Bronny for the time being remains on the Lakers' roster, set to play his third year on a four-year contract that he signed in 2024. The 21-year-old became a rotation player by the end of last season, garnering 16.9 minutes per game while appearing in eight playoff games with the Lakers.

But president Bob Myers and the Philadelphia 76ers should happily acquire Bronny. Here are three reasons why.

Is Bronny James a good NBA player? I don't think anyone would argue that he is right now. The better framework is to count him among the hundred or so players who are trying to make it in the league. In 556 minutes over two seasons, he's averaging 2.7 points, 1.1 assists and 0.6 rebounds. Not great. On a per-minute basis, his career PER of 8.4 is 464th among 485 players with at least 500 minutes over the last two seasons. Still: not great.

But he's trending upward. The swing skill for Bronny is his 3-point shot, which would allow him to level up his athleticism with a perimeter threat. Last season, he made 22 of his 57 3-point shots, giving him a promising 38.6% conversion rate, an improvement from his debut mark of 28.1%. If he can maintain a strong percentage and continue to deliver strong on-ball defense, he'll be able to carve out a role as an NBA player.

There's also G-League data. In his age-20 and age-21 seasons, his G-League ledger shows that there's something there. In 25 career games in the G-League, Bronny is averaging 18.4 points, 4.4 assists and 4.0 rebounds in 30 minutes per game while shooting 49.6% from the floor, 41.3% on six 3-pointers per game and 80.5% from the line. For a defensive-minded player like Bronny, scoring 22 points per 36 minutes with an above-average 63.9% true shooting percentage at the G-League suggests he's more than ready for NBA minutes.

Maybe Bronny doesn't pan out to be a Top 300 player one day. Gary Payton II bounced around the league before he found a real home in Golden State at age 29. Bronny is eight years younger than GP2 and, despite his youth, teams will have hundreds of millions of reasons to employ Bronny and his father.

He's already proven he's worthy of a roster spot. If you're annoyed by the nepotism at play, NBA history tells us that league executives have to pay off a debt to sons of NBA players who deserved better shots.

Do you remember Mladen Sekularac?

How about Cady Lalanne, Herbert Hill, Ejike Ugboaja, Rick Rickert, Maurice Jeffers, Kris Clack and Ronnie Henderson?

These names are among the 31 No. 55 selections since the draft expanded to that many picks in 1996. Which means that one out of every four No. 55s don't even make it to Game No. 1.

That's the thing about Bronny James. Players selected this late in the draft are basically blind dart throws, unlikely to make any impact in the league whatsoever.

Any Bronny analysis has to begin with the recognition of the longshot baseline, one that shows playing in a single game is already an accomplishment. Anything after that is cake. Consider this fact: in just two seasons, Bronny has already scored the 12th-most career points of the 31 selections at No. 55.

Lakers head coach JJ Redick gave Bronny his big opportunity at the end of last season, playing him real minutes as a fringe rotation player on a playoff team. That just doesn't usually happen for players drafted as late as he was, as young as he was. In fact, among the 144 players drafted since 2000 at the No. 55 slot or later, only 15 actually played by their age-21 season, or what amounts to about 10%, according to Stathead.com research tools. Bronny is getting minutes earlier than 90% of those who are drafted as late as he was. Through this lens, Bronny is ahead of the curve.

Did Bronny benefit from being LeBron James' son and get an earlier opportunity? Sure, but such a nepotistic benefit is long overdue considering that second-generation players have been snubbed more often than not in the past. The NBA draft tells the story that NBA progeny has been underrated.

In a span beginning with the modern two-round draft's debut in 1989 and 2022, there have been 62 players selected who were the sons of an NBA player. Some became future Hall of Famers, including Stephen Curry, Kobe Bryant and Jalen Brunson. Others became perennial All-Stars and champions, including Kevin Love, Al Horford and Klay Thompson.

As I pointed out last month advocating for Carlos Boozer's son, Cam, for the No. 1 pick, sons of NBA players are nearly twice as likely to become All-Stars than their non-legacy counterparts. The reality is that sons of NBA players like Bronny James have seemingly been punished, or at the very least overlooked, by teams for having a father who played in the league.

Despite their family's starpower, Scotty Pippen Jr., Gary Payton II and Seth Curry never heard their names called on draft night and have played a combined 26 seasons in the league. Even for second-generation players who don't have a box-office last name like Luke Kornet, Garrett Temple and Wesley Matthews, the fact that their fathers played in the NBA wasn't enough to get picked.

Punished might seem like too strong of a word, but the successes of undrafted sons of NBA players lends credence to the idea that GMs stiff the name-brand prospect, preferring instead to go for lesser-known diamonds in the rough that may make them look smarter for discovering. Like GP2 and Seth Curry, it took a while for some smaller second-gen players to carve out their NBA role. Considering that Bob Myers is playing with house money getting LeBron James at just the veteran minimum this season, trading for Bronny would be a no-brainer.

It's totally possible that this was part of the deal with Philly: If I sign for the minimum, commit to trading for Bronny and I'm in. So far, there's no indication that Bronny and LeBron is a package deal, but if LeBron's happiness was truly the North Star that brought him to Philly and he wants to continue playing with his son, the Sixers' business and basketball ops shouldn't think twice about doing LeBron a solid.

LeBron James has made $584 million in his NBA career. That's a bargain. Because of the max contract that artificially caps the earning power of the best players, James has effectively subsidized the contracts of the rest of his NBA peers while providing enormous surplus value for his squad.

In a 2024 study, a BYU economist Scott Kaplan showed that James' predicted salary in 2018-19 based on ticket sales, merchandise, popularity (as represented by All-Star votes) and player performance would be a whopping $123.3 million, nearly $100 million higher than his actual salary paid by the Lakers that season ($35.6 million). And that's just value to the Lakers. Kaplan asserted that due to James' ability to fill seats on the road, his value to the entire league was worth an annualized $229 million in salary.

Instead of James getting that money, it's distributed as part of the BRI (basketball-related income) to other players. Call it the LeBron James Subsidy. Nowadays, LeBron, at 41, doesn't spin up quite as much box-office magic as he did back then when he regularly led all players in All-Star votes.

Last season marked the first time in 22 years that he wasn't voted as a starter, but he still finished with the eighth-most votes in the league. By comparison, in 2018-19, Kevin Durant ranked eighth in All-Star votes and, according to Kaplan's model, provided $182 million in value to the NBA, with $98 million allocated directly to his team.

So what will LeBron be worth in 2026-27 as a Sixer? Let's throw in the fact that the cap has skyrocketed about 60% higher than it was in 2018-19. With revenues more frothy than at the time of Kaplan's study, we can roughly project James' predicted salary for his new team to be over $150 million and nearly $300 million in total value for the NBA. And that's pegging his value to a player ranking eighth in All-Star votes like KD in 2019.

So, yeah, James' economic value to his new team will dwarf his contract, and that was before he indicated that he was willing to play for the veteran's minimum of $3.9 million. Bronny's contract will pay him $2.3 million next season which is a rounding error compared to what James' on-court and off-court value will provide. Honestly, if Bronny's younger siblings Bryce and Zhuri were both old enough and entered the draft, teams would probably consider employing them too.

Bronny remains on the Lakers roster, but the team needs to trim at least one player in order to be in line with league roster rules. By going over the roster limit, Luka's team appears to be operating as if Bronny is expendable. Perhaps they truly believe he's the next GP2, the scrappy son of an NBA player that needed a few years to find his footing, and they find a way to keep him around. But they probably know he's worth more to LeBron's new team than his old one.

Both the Lakers and Sixers have some cap work to do. According to ESPN's Bobby Marks, Philadelphia is currently $572,000 above the first apron, so they have to shed salary. Dominick Barlow's $3.4 million for Bronny's $2.3 million would get them there. It might make more sense to find a home for Dalen Terry, who is already in a logjam in the backcourt before Bronny comes into the picture.

Maybe the Lakers play hardball with the Sixers and ask for a, um, King's ransom, but then again, no team drafted him early and made the Lakers sweat in 2024 despite everyone who paid one second of attention to draft coverage knowing the Lakers would seriously consider drafting Bronny at 55.

Is Bronny getting more opportunities because of his name? Probably. But he's the exception to the rule. Usually, sons of NBA players are snubbed rather than spoonfed. LeBron is the only one who stuck around long enough to make sure the second-generation snub didn't happen to his family. After all, Philadelphia is the City of Brotherly Love. LeBron and Bronny could make Fatherly Love a reality.
